claims.text: The studied material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The as-fabricated alloy has an FCC matrix.
Additive-manufacturing rapid solidification introduces microstructural heterogeneities into the alloy.
Degradation in an oxidizing atmosphere is governed by formation of a continuous but brittle oxide scale.
The oxide scale concentrates stress at microstructural heterogeneities.
Oxide-induced stress concentration accelerates microcrack initiation.
Oxidizing exposure causes earlier catastrophic failure than reducing exposure.
Oxide-scale continuity at grain boundaries and other microstructural heterogeneities is the relevant structural mediator.
The oxide layer formed under oxidizing conditions is rich in alumina and chromium oxides.
Reducing conditions slow oxidation relative to oxidizing conditions.
Accumulated oxidation-related stresses eventually cause catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a more continuous and brittle oxide scale than the comparator atmosphere.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a higher local microcrack density than the comparator atmosphere.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce time to failure relative to the comparator atmosphere.
The proposed behavior is most pronounced from approximately 600°C to 800°C.
Exposure outside 600°C to 800°C may have different oxidation kinetics or degradation mechanisms.
The initial alloy has minimal oxidation before elevated-temperature exposure.
Comparing nominally identical samples in oxygen-rich and inert atmospheres during thermal cycling at 700°C is proposed as the controlled test.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires comparison with reducing conditions, but the proposed comparator is an inert gas. An inert atmosphere is not necessarily chemically reducing, so the experimental control does not unambiguously implement the claimed oxidizing-versus-reducing contrast.
